planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions or rooted stem-tip cuttings in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring; shining clubmoss depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi and almost never survives transplanting from wild-collected material, so source only nursery-grown stock.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions or rooted stem-tip cuttings in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring; shining clubmoss depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi and almost never survives transplanting from wild-collected material, so source only nursery-grown stock. This evergreen fern ally forms low, glossy, dark-green tufts of forking stems clothed in narrow, shining, needle-like leaflets, spreading slowly by both creeping stems and leaf-tip gemmae that fall and root nearby. It is a signature groundcover of cool, moist, undisturbed eastern hardwood and hemlock forests and reads as a miniature, evergreen conifer at the forest floor, pairing well with partridgeberry and wood ferns. Keep soil constantly moist and never let it dry out or sit in standing water; it resents heat, drought, and disturbed or compacted ground.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown rooted rhizome sections in acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil under open pine or oak canopy in spring; fan clubmoss forms a mycorrhizal partnership with soil fungi and colonies transplanted from the wild rarely establish, so treat it as a slow, long-term planting from certified nursery stock.

directions: Plant nursery-grown rooted rhizome sections in acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil under open pine or oak canopy in spring; fan clubmoss forms a mycorrhizal partnership with soil fungi and colonies transplanted from the wild rarely establish, so treat it as a slow, long-term planting from certified nursery stock. Long, horizontal above-ground runners send up flattened, fan-shaped, evergreen branches that closely resemble a miniature cedar seedling, gradually knitting together into broad woodland-floor colonies once established. It is the clubmoss most often cut for holiday greenery ('running cedar') in the eastern and southeastern United States, and heavy wild harvesting has made established colonies increasingly scarce, so cultivated plantings help take pressure off native stands. Once rooted it tolerates the light, dappled shade and dry-to-average duff of upland pine-oak woods with little care.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rooted stem sections in acidic, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; running clubmoss is mycorrhizal-dependent and slow to establish, so give it undisturbed ground and patience rather than fertilizer.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rooted stem sections in acidic, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; running clubmoss is mycorrhizal-dependent and slow to establish, so give it undisturbed ground and patience rather than fertilizer. Trailing, densely leafy stems creep along the ground and root at intervals, sending up forking, candelabra-like branches tipped in narrow yellow-green spore-bearing 'candles' in mid- to late summer. One of the most widely distributed clubmosses in the Northern Hemisphere, it colonizes acidic woodland edges, old pastures, and cutover forest with a mossy, evergreen texture unlike any true moss or fern. Its spores are extremely fine and oily and were historically collected commercially as flash powder and pill-coating dust, but home plantings are grown strictly as an unusual, low-maintenance groundcover.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in acidic, moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade in spring; ground pine relies on mycorrhizal fungi in undisturbed forest duff and transplants slowly even under good conditions.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in acidic, moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade in spring; ground pine relies on mycorrhizal fungi in undisturbed forest duff and transplants slowly even under good conditions. Upright, repeatedly branched stems clothed in tiny, glossy, dark-green scale-like leaves rise from long underground rhizomes and closely resemble a miniature evergreen conifer sapling, giving rise to the common names 'ground pine' and 'princess pine.' It spreads into loose, scattered colonies across the floor of mature, cool hardwood and mixed forests and was historically overharvested for Christmas wreaths and garlands, so cultivated plantings are valued for taking pressure off wild stands. Leave leaf litter in place and avoid soil disturbance, fertilizer, or lime, all of which it tolerates poorly.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in moist, rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade in spring; rattlesnake fern is mycorrhizal-dependent and very slow-growing from spores, so start only from nursery-grown crowns and expect a long establishment period.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in moist, rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade in spring; rattlesnake fern is mycorrhizal-dependent and very slow-growing from spores, so start only from nursery-grown crowns and expect a long establishment period. Each plant sends up a single broad, finely divided, lacy sterile blade in early spring, from the base of which a separate upright fertile stalk emerges bearing a branched cluster of bead-like spore cases that resembles a rattlesnake's rattle once it browns in summer. It is one of the earliest ferns to unfurl in rich deciduous woods each spring and disappears by mid- to late summer once spores are shed, so mark its location or interplant with later-emerging shade perennials to avoid bare patches. Undisturbed leaf litter and consistent moisture through spring are essential to its survival.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to filtered sun in spring; adder's-tongue fern is mycorrhizal-dependent, easy to overlook, and slow to increase, so mark plantings clearly and avoid disturbing the soil around them.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to filtered sun in spring; adder's-tongue fern is mycorrhizal-dependent, easy to overlook, and slow to increase, so mark plantings clearly and avoid disturbing the soil around them. Each plant produces just a single smooth, undivided, oval sterile blade with a separate slender fertile spike rising from its base, tipped with a row of embedded spore cases that suggest a snake's tongue — a form unlike any typical fern. It grows in damp meadows, fens, and open moist woodland edges, going dormant underground for much of the year and reappearing only briefly each growing season, so patience and consistent soil moisture matter more than active care. Because populations are small and easily lost to mowing or soil compaction, it is best grown in a protected, undisturbed corner of a shade or bog garden.

planting.note: Direct sow onto exposed wet mud or very moist, fertile, high-organic-matter soil near pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens from a few weeks before last frost through late summer; marsh yellowcress is a watercress relative that germinates readily on bare damp ground and needs constant moisture, not standing shade.

directions: Direct sow onto exposed wet mud or very moist, fertile, high-organic-matter soil near pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens from a few weeks before last frost through late summer; marsh yellowcress is a watercress relative that germinates readily on bare damp ground and needs constant moisture, not standing shade. This fast-growing native annual to short-lived perennial forms rosettes of glossy, deeply lobed leaves with a mild, peppery, watercress-like bite that is best harvested young, before the small four-petaled yellow flowers and narrow seed pods appear on branching stems. It thrives on disturbed, muddy, nutrient-rich ground such as pond margins, streambanks, and seasonally flooded low spots where few other food crops will grow, self-sows readily, and can be treated as a cut-and-come-again green through a moist summer. Harvest leaves regularly to delay bolting and keep the planting from spreading beyond the intended wet area.

planting.note: Start seed indoors requiring cold-moist stratification or plant nursery divisions in wet to consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral soil in partial shade in spring; swamp saxifrage is a wetland-edge native that wants boggy ground, not average garden soil.

directions: Start seed indoors requiring cold-moist stratification or plant nursery divisions in wet to consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral soil in partial shade in spring; swamp saxifrage is a wetland-edge native that wants boggy ground, not average garden soil. A basal rosette of broad, coarsely toothed leaves sends up a tall, sticky-hairy flower stalk in mid-spring bearing loose, branched clusters of small, star-shaped, greenish-white to purple-tinged flowers that are an early-season draw for small bees and flies. It occurs naturally in wet meadows, marsh edges, and seepage areas and is an easy, low-maintenance choice for the damp, partly shaded margins of a rain garden or pond where turf grass struggles. It is monocarpic in some populations, flowering once from a mature rosette and then dying back, but self-sows readily to persist in a consistently moist planting.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; downy Solomon's seal spreads gradually by rhizome and resents being disturbed once established.

directions: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; downy Solomon's seal spreads gradually by rhizome and resents being disturbed once established. Smaller and more delicate than the more commonly grown giant and smooth Solomon's seals, this eastern woodland native carries arching stems of paired, softly downy-veined leaves and pairs of small, greenish-yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling beneath the foliage in late spring, followed by blue-black berries. It naturalizes slowly into loose colonies in rich deciduous forest and pairs well with trilliums, wild ginger, and ferns in a woodland border, offering a finer, more compact texture than its larger relatives where space is limited. Top-dress with leaf mold each fall rather than fertilizing, and keep soil from drying out during summer.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade in spring; western maidenhair naturally roots into rocky streambank seeps and appreciates a gritty, well-aerated planting mix.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade in spring; western maidenhair naturally roots into rocky streambank seeps and appreciates a gritty, well-aerated planting mix. Wiry, glossy blackish-purple stems fan out into delicate, finely divided, blue-green fronds in a distinctive upright, hand-shaped arrangement, giving the plant a more architectural, vase-like habit than the similar eastern maidenhair fern. Native to moist, rocky slopes, cliff seeps, and streambanks from Alaska south through the Pacific coast ranges and disjunct populations in the East, it is a choice specimen for a shaded rock garden, waterfall edge, or container where its fine texture and dark stems can be appreciated up close. Keep soil evenly moist and sheltered from drying wind, and mulch lightly with leaf litter over winter in colder zones.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions inside a buried rhizome barrier in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this running bamboo spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and needs physical containment in any garden setting.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions inside a buried rhizome barrier in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this running bamboo spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and needs physical containment in any garden setting. Thick, upright canes carry unusually broad, glossy, deep-green leaves up to a foot long that bleach an attractive straw color at the margins in winter, giving the clump a bold, coarse, tropical texture unlike typical fine-leaved bamboos. It is one of the most shade-tolerant bamboos available and colonizes dry shade, deep shade under trees, and difficult slopes where turf and most groundcovers fail, making it useful for erosion control or as a dense screen in problem shaded sites — but only where its spread can be fully contained. Cut old canes to the ground in late winter to refresh the clump and control height.

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; gopher plant is a dryland Mediterranean spurge that rots quickly in humid, poorly drained soil and is best raised in beds or on slopes in wetter climates.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; gopher plant is a dryland Mediterranean spurge that rots quickly in humid, poorly drained soil and is best raised in beds or on slopes in wetter climates. Thick, upright stems radiate in whorls of narrow, fleshy, blue-gray leaves year-round, topped in late winter and early spring by dense clusters of long-lasting, chartreuse-yellow bracts that provide some of the earliest bold color in a xeriscape or gravel garden. Extremely drought-tolerant once established and reputed to repel gophers and deer, it is a striking textural and color contrast plant for rock gardens, dry slopes, and raised xeriscape beds, but its milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves when pruning or dividing. Cut spent flowering stems to the base after bloom to keep the clump tidy and encourage fresh growth.
